title: Dzhokhar Dudayev
short_description: First President of the Chechen Republic of Ichkeria

content: **Dzhokhar Musayevich Dudayev** (born **Dudin Musa-Khant Dzhokhar**;[a][b] 15 February 1944 – 21 April 1996) was a Chechen politician, revolutionary and military leader of the 1990s Chechen independence movement from Russia. He served as the first president of the [Chechen Republic of Ichkeria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chechen_Republic_of_Ichkeria) from 1991 until his assassination in 1996. Dudayev had previously served as a senior officer in the [Soviet Air Forces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_Air_Forces).

Dudayev was born in Chechnya in 1944, days before his family and the entire Chechen nation were [deported to Central Asia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deportation_of_the_Chechens_and_Ingush) by the Soviet regime in the [Chechen genocide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chechen_genocide) as part of an [ethnic cleansing program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_deportations) which affected several million members of ethnic minorities in the Soviet Union between the 1930s and 1950s. His family was allowed to return to his native Chechnya in 1956, after [Joseph Stalin’s death](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Death_and_state_funeral_of_Joseph_Stalin). From 1962, Dudayev served in the Soviet Air Forces, reaching the rank of major general. He commanded strategic nuclear bomber aircraft divisions based in [Poltava](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poltava) and [Tartu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tartu), and was awarded several [state orders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_order) of the Soviet Union, most notably the [Order of the Red Banner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_of_the_Red_Banner) and the [Order of the Red Star](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_of_the_Red_Star).

In 1991, Dudayev refused orders from Moscow to suppress [Estonia's independence movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Singing_Revolution), and subsequently resigned from the [Soviet Armed Forces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_Armed_Forces) before returning to Chechnya. He became president of the Chechen Republic of Ichkeria after a referendum in October 1991, and unilaterally declared the republic's independence from the Soviet Union. In the [First Chechen War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Chechen_War) (1994–1996), Dudayev organized a successful resistance against Russian forces before he was assassinated by a Russian airstrike. [Grozny](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grozny), the capital of Chechnya, was renamed Dzhokhar-Ghala in Dudayev's honor between 1996 and 2005.

sections.heading: Early life and military career
content: Dudayev was born in [Yalkhoroy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yalkhoroy) from the Tsechoy [teip](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teip) in the [Checheno-Ingush Autonomous Soviet Socialist Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Checheno-Ingush_Autonomous_Soviet_Socialist_Republic) (ASSR), just a few days before the [forced deportation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deportation_of_the_Chechens_and_Ingush) of his family together with the entire [Chechen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chechen_people) population on the orders of [Lavrentiy Beria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lavrentiy_Beria). He was the thirteenth youngest child of veterinarian Musa and Rabiat Dudayev. He spent the first 13 years of his life in internal exile in the [Kazakh Soviet Socialist Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kazakh_Soviet_Socialist_Republic). His family was only able to return to Chechnya in 1957.[4] Following the 1957 [repatriation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Repatriation) of the Chechens, he studied at evening school in Checheno-Ingushetia and qualified as an electrician. In 1962, after two years studying [electronics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electronics) in [Vladikavkaz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vladikavkaz), he entered the [Tambov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tambov) Higher Military Aviation School for Pilots from which he graduated in 1966. Dudayev joined the [Communist Party of the Soviet Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Communist_Party_of_the_Soviet_Union) in 1968 and from 1971 to 1974 studied at the prestigious [Gagarin Air Force Academy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gagarin_Air_Force_Academy). He married [Alla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alla_Dudayeva), a Russian [poet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poet) and the daughter of a Soviet officer, with whom he had three children (a daughter and two sons).[4]

In 1962, Dudayev began serving in the [Soviet Air Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_Air_Force) where he rose to the rank of Major-General, becoming its first Chechen general. Dudayev served in a [strategic bombing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strategic_bombing) unit of the Soviet Air Force in [Siberia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siberia) and [Ukraine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ukrainian_SSR). He allegedly participated in the [Soviet–Afghan War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet–Afghan_War) against the [Mujahideen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mujahideen), for which he was awarded the [Order of the Red Star](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_of_the_Red_Star) and the [Order of the Red Banner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_of_the_Red_Banner).[5] Reportedly from 1986 to 1987, Dudayev had participated in bombing raids in western Afghanistan. Dudayev had stated he was a "dedicated Muslim."[6] He politically stressed Chechen nationalism as president. Many of his military and political opponents who questioned his Muslim faith often made reference to his actions against the Mujahideen forces.[7][8] For example, [Sergei Stepashin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sergei_Stepashin) asserted Dudayev participated in [carpet bombing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carpet_bombing) (a statement probably motivated by spite).[9][10] These allegations were denied by Dudayev himself.[11] Dudayev rose steadily in the Air Force, assuming command of the [326th Heavy Bomber Aviation Division](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/326th_Heavy_Bomber_Aviation_Division) of the [Soviet Long Range Aviation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_Long_Range_Aviation) at [Tartu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tartu), [Estonia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estonian_Soviet_Socialist_Republic), in 1987 gaining the rank of [Major-General](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Major-General). From 1987 to March 1990, he commanded [nuclear-armed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_weapon) long-range [strategic bombers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strategic_bomber) during his post there.[9][12][c]

He was also commander of the garrison of Tartu. He learned [Estonian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estonian_language) and showed great tolerance for [restoration of Estonian independence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estonian_Restoration_of_Independence) when in autumn 1990 he ignored the orders (as commander of the garrison of Tartu) to shut down the Estonian television and parliament.[4][9] In 1990, his air [division](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Division_(military)) was withdrawn from Estonia and Dudayev resigned from the [Soviet military](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_military).

sections.heading: Chechen politics
content: In May 1990, Dudayev returned to [Grozny](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grozny), the Chechen capital, to devote himself to local politics. He was elected head of the Executive Committee of the unofficial opposition [All-National Congress of the Chechen People](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/All-National_Congress_of_the_Chechen_People) (NCChP), which advocated [sovereignty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sovereignty) for Chechnya as a separate [republic of the Soviet Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republics_of_the_Soviet_Union) (the Chechen-Ingush ASSR had the status of an [autonomous republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autonomous_republic) of the [Russian Soviet Federative Socialist Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_Soviet_Federative_Socialist_Republic)).

In August 1991, [Doku Zavgayev](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doku_Zavgayev), the Communist leader of the Chechen-Ingush ASSR, did not publicly condemn the [August 1991 attempted coup d'état](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1991_Soviet_coup_d'état_attempt) against Soviet president [Mikhail Gorbachev](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mikhail_Gorbachev). Following the failure of the [putsch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coup_d'état#Putsch), the Soviet Union [began to disintegrate rapidly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_of_the_Soviet_Union) as the constituent republics took moves to leave the beleaguered Soviet Union. Taking advantage of the Soviet Union's implosion, Dudayev and his supporters acted against the Zavgayev administration. On 6 September 1991, the militants of the NCChP violently (the Grozny Communist party leader was killed and several other members were wounded) invaded a session of the local [Supreme Soviet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supreme_Soviet), effectively dissolving the government of the Chechen-Ingush ASSR. Grozny television station and other key government buildings were also taken over. Dudayev and his supporters stated that the [revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chechen_Revolution) had occurred and that the revolutionary committee would assume all power before the snap presidential elections.

sections.heading: President of the Chechen Republic of Ichkeria
content: After a referendum in October 1991 confirmed Dudayev in his new position as president of the [Chechen Republic of Ichkeria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chechen_Republic_of_Ichkeria), he declared the republic's sovereignty and its independence from the Russian Federation. In November 1991, the then [Russian president](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_president) [Boris Yeltsin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boris_Yeltsin) dispatched troops to Grozny, but they were withdrawn when Dudayev's forces prevented them from leaving the airport. Russia refused to recognize the republic's independence, but hesitated to use further force against the separatists. From this point, the Checheno-Ingush Republic had become a *[de facto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/De_facto)* independent state.

Initially, Dudayev's government had diplomatic relations with [Georgia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_(country)) where he received much moral support from the first Georgian president [Zviad Gamsakhurdia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zviad_Gamsakhurdia). When Gamsakhurdia was overthrown in late 1991, he was given [asylum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Right_of_asylum) in Chechnya and attended Dudayev's inauguration as President. While he resided in Grozny he also helped to organise the first "All-Caucasian Conference" which was attended by independentist groups from across the region. Ichkeria never received diplomatic recognition from any internationally recognised state other than Georgia in 1991.

The Chechen-Ingush Republic split in two in June 1992, amidst the increasing [Ossetian-Ingush conflict](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ossetian-Ingush_conflict). After Chechnya had announced its initial declaration of sovereignty in 1991, its former entity [Ingushetia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ingushetia) opted to join the Russian Federation as a [federal subject](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_subjects_of_Russia) (Republic of Ingushetia). The remaining rump state of [Ichkeria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chechen_Republic_of_Ichkeria) (Chechnya) declared full independence in 1993. That same year the Russian language stopped being taught in Chechen schools and it was also announced that the [Chechen language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chechen_language) would start to be written using the [Latin alphabet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_alphabet) (with some additional special Chechen characters) rather than [Cyrillic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyrillic_script) in use since the 1930s. The state also began to print its own money and stamps. One of Dudayev's first decrees gave every man the [right to bear arms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Right_to_arms).

In 1993, the Chechen parliament attempted to organize a referendum on public confidence in Dudayev on the grounds that he had failed to consolidate Chechnya's independence. He retaliated by dissolving parliament and other organs of power. Beginning in early summer of 1994, armed Chechen opposition groups with [Russian military](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_military) and financial backing tried repeatedly but without success to depose Dudayev by force.

sections.heading: First Chechen War
content: On 1 December 1994, the Russians began bombing [Grozny airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Dolinskoye) and destroyed some former Soviet training aircraft taken away by the republic in 1991. In response, Ichkeria mobilised its [armed forces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Chechen_War). On 11 December 1994, five days after Dudayev and Minister of Defense [Pavel Grachev](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pavel_Grachev) of Russia had agreed to avoid the further use of force, Russian troops invaded Chechnya.

Before the fall of Grozny, Dudayev abandoned [the presidential palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidential_Palace,_Grozny), moved south with his forces and continued leading the war throughout 1995, reportedly from a [missile silo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Missile_silo) close to the historic Chechen capital of [Vedeno](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vedeno). He continued to insist that his forces would prevail after the [conventional warfare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conventional_warfare) had finished, and the Chechen [guerrilla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guerrilla_warfare) fighters continued to operate across the entire republic. The full-scale Russian attack led many of Dudayev's opponents to side with his forces and thousands of volunteers to swell the ranks of mobile militant units.

sections.heading: Assassination
content: On 21 April 1996, while using a [satellite phone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satellite_phone), Dudayev was assassinated by two [laser-guided](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laser-guided) [missiles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Missile), after his location was detected by a Russian [reconnaissance aircraft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reconnaissance_aircraft), which intercepted his phone call.[14] At the time, Dudayev was talking to [Konstantin Borovoi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Konstantin_Borovoi), a deputy of the [State Duma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_Duma) in [Moscow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moscow).[15] Additional aircraft were dispatched (a single [Su-24MR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sukhoi_Su-24) and a single [Su-25](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Su-25)) to locate Dudayev and fire a guided missile. Exact details of this operation have not been released by the Russian government. Russian [reconnaissance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reconnaissance) planes in the area had been monitoring [satellite communications](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satellite_communications) for some time trying to match Dudayev's voice signature to the existing samples of his speech. It was claimed Dudayev was killed by a combination of an [airstrike](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Airstrike) and a [booby trap](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Booby_trap). He was 52 years old.[16]

The death of Dudayev was announced on the interrupted television [broadcast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Broadcast) by [Shamil Basayev](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shamil_Basayev), the Chechen guerrilla commander.[17] Dudayev was succeeded by his [Vice-President](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice-President) [Zelimkhan Yandarbiyev](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zelimkhan_Yandarbiyev) (as [acting president](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acting_president)) and then, after the 1997 popular elections, by his wartime [Chief of Staff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chief_of_Staff), [Aslan Maskhadov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aslan_Maskhadov).
Dudayev was survived by his wife, Alla, and their sons.

sections.heading: Commemoration
content: There is a memorial plaque made of granite attached to the house on 8 [Ülikooli street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ülikooli_street), [Tartu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tartu), Estonia, in which Dudayev used to work.[18] The house now hosts Hotel Barclay, and the former office of Dudayev has been converted into Dudayev's Room.[19]
Places named in honor of Dudayev include:
[Georgia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_(country)) – There is a street in the Georgian capital [Tbilisi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tbilisi) named after Dzokhar Dudayev.[20]

[Latvia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latvia) – In 1996, a street in the Latvian capital [Riga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riga) was named **Džohara Dudajeva gatve** (Dzhokhar Dudaev Street). In the light of the upcoming Parliamentary elections in Latvia, several initiatives have been undertaken to lobby for the renaming or preserving the name of the street by pro-Russian and [anti-Russian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russophobia#Latvia) political parties respectively.[21][22]

[Lithuania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lithuania) – **Džocharo Dudajevo skveras** (Dzhokhar Dudaev Square) in the [Žvėrynas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Žvėrynas) district of [Vilnius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vilnius).[23]

[Poland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poland) – On 17 March 2005, a [roundabout](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roundabout) in the Polish capital [Warsaw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warsaw) was named **Rondo Dżochara Dudajewa** (Dzhokhar Dudayev Roundabout).[24]

[Turkey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turkey) – After Dudayev's death, various locations in Turkey were renamed after him, such as **Şehit Cahar Dudayev Caddesi** (Martyr Dzhokhar Dudayev Avenue) and **Şehit Cahar Dudayev Parkı** (Martyr Dzhokhar Dudayev Park) in Istanbul/Ataşehir-Örnek, **Cahar Dudayev Meydanı** (Dzhokhar Dudayev Square) in [Ankara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ankara), **Şehit Cahar Dudayev Parkı** (Martyr Dzhokhar Dudaev Park) in Adapazarı, [Sakarya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sakarya_Province) and **Şehit Cevher Dudayev Parkı** in [Sivas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sivas).[25]

[Ukraine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ukraine) – In 1996, a street in [Lviv](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lviv) was named *вулиця Джохара Дудаєва* (Dzhokhar Dudayev Street), later followed by a street in [Ivano-Frankivsk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivano-Frankivsk)[26][27] and a street in [Khmelnytskyi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khmelnytskyi,_Ukraine).[28] In the [war in Donbas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_in_Donbas_(2014–2022)), that started in the spring of 2014, a [pro-Ukrainian volunteer battalion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dzhokhar_Dudayev_Battalion) was named after Dudayev, led by former Chechen General [Isa Munayev](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isa_Munayev).[26] In December 2022 [recently liberated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Kharkiv_counteroffensive) (from [Russian forces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_invasion_of_Ukraine)) [Izium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Izium) decided to rename [Turgenev](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivan_Turgenev) Street to Dzhokhar Dudayev Street.[29] In May 2023 [Poltava](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poltava) renamed [Nikitchenko](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikolai_Nikitchenko) Street in honor of Dzhokhar Dudayev.[30][31] In June 2026 [Kharkiv](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kharkiv) renamed [Kubanska](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kuban) Street to Dzhokhar Dudayev Street.[32]

content: a. [Chechen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chechen_language): ДудагӀеран Мусан-воӀ ЖовхӀар, romanized: *Dudaġeran Musan-voj Ƶhovhar*; [Russian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_language): Джохар Мусаевич Дудаев; [US pronunciation](https://en.wikipedia.org.org/wikipedia/commons/transcoded/0/0b/En-us-Dzhokar_Dudayev_from_Chechnya_pronunciation_%28Voice_of_America%29.ogg/En-us-Dzhokar_Dudayev_from_Chechnya_pronunciation_%28Voice_of_America%29.ogg.mp3)[ⓘ](https://en.wikipedia.orgzhokar_Dudayev_from_Chechnya_pronunciation_(Voice_of_America).ogg)
b. The spelling of Dudayev's given name in modern Chechen ranges between Джохар, ДжовхӀар, Джовхар and Жовхар.

c. While Dudayev was in Chechnya in the 1990s, his family lived at 21-52 Sõpruse Boulevard ([Estonian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estonian_language): *Sõpruse puiestee 21-52*) which was his the residence while he commanded the 326th Heavy Bomber Aviation Division in Tartu.[13]
